figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: EO-Jev is more accurate, better calibrated and faster. Centre: mean accuracy per capability (30 benchmarks). Corners: real questions with each model’s answer and confidence; footers give benchmark accuracy (specialist $\rightarrow$ EO-Jev) and throughput vs. the specialist. Bottom: per-capability medians of accuracy gain and throughput vs. the best specialist, and ECE drop vs. d3-flash; green = better, red = worse.
figures.headline: Per-capability medians show EO-Jev gaining accuracy and throughput over specialists and lowering calibration error relative to d3-flash.
citing_sentences: For EO applications such as damage triage, monitoring and alerting, this is an attractive capability as an answer that comes with a trustworthy confidence can be thresholded, aggregated and audited, as illustrated in Figure 1, whereas free-form text generated auto-regressively cannot.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: EO-Jev Architecture and Training. EO images (single images, pre/post pairs or time series) are paired with typed questions with predefined answers. General decision data is replayed in 20% of each batch. The vision encoder and text tower $\Phi_{\theta}$ process the images and questions, respectively. A frozen readout $W_{r}$ converts the final hidden state $h$ into option probabilities $p$. Training: LoRA adapters in the vision encoder and text tower are optimized using KL divergence against target distributions $q$, with an additional ranked probability score (RPS) on ordinal questions. Inference: merged adapters ($W+BA$) enable single-pass predictions at d3-flash cost. Answers are accepted when confidence exceeds a per-question threshold $\tau_{q}$ and otherwise deferred to an analyst. Examples and probabilities are illustrative.
figures.headline: EO-Jev trains adapters against target distributions, then merges them so inference costs the same as d3-flash.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 summarizes how we adapt d3-flash to Earth observation.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Qualitative examples across capability groups. Each panel shows the input image(s), the question and its options (gold option highlighted in green), and the top answer of each model with its probability, or “written” for specialists whose best mode is a generated answer. Badges: I = in-domain, O = out-of-domain for EO-Jev. In (b)–(g), d3-flash sometimes answers incorrectly with high confidence, defined as assigning a probability of at least 0.8 to the selected answer (e.g., predicting the Americas for an Oceanian site in (f)), the color cannot be determined in (g)), while EO-Jev selects the correct option; in (d) and (f) the best specialist is wrong as well. This includes two out-of-domain settings, NWPU VHR-10 counting (c) and VHM deceptive questions (g), where no training image came from the benchmark’s dataset. Panel (a) is an out-of-domain scene that every model answers correctly, EO-Jev with $p=1.00$. All images, questions and probabilities are taken unchanged from the evaluation runs.
figures.headline: d3-flash answers some examples confidently wrong where EO-Jev is correct, including two out-of-domain counting and abstention cases.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 shows one example per capability group, including two out-of-domain cases (counting on NWPU VHR-10 and abstention on VHM deceptive questions) that EO-Jev answers correctly while d3-flash does not.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Calibration change from d3-flash to EO-Jev. Each arrow runs from d3-flash’s ECE (open circle) to EO-Jev’s (filled circle); lower is better. Rows are grouped by $\Delta$ECE $=$ EO-Jev $-$ d3-flash: much better calibrated ($\Delta$ECE $\leq-0.05$), better calibrated, no significant change, and worse calibrated. ∗: the paired 95% bootstrap interval (over images) excludes zero. Badges: I = in-domain, O = out-of-domain, G = general (non-EO) retention check. All EO rows in the bottom tier are over-confident; the Decision Index is slightly under-confident.
figures.headline: Most EO settings move to lower calibration error for EO-Jev, while the settings that get worse are all overconfident.
citing_sentences: As Figure 4 shows, EO-Jev has significantly lower ECE than d3-flash on 17 of 30 EO settings, higher on 5, and no significant change on 8.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Inference cost against the specialists. (a) Specialist median latency per question as a multiple of EO-Jev’s, one question per call. (b) EO-Jev throughput as a multiple of the specialist’s, each at its best batch size. Bars are grouped by speed-up; red rows are those where the specialist is faster. Badges give the specialist’s best-accuracy mode (P: prompted, W: wrapped/generative). All models run on the same exclusive node (4$\times$A100, BF16), on the same 160-question seeded sample per row, with image decoding inside the timed region. Medians: 3.2$\times$ in (a) and 6.4$\times$ in (b).
figures.headline: EO-Jev is a median 3.2 times faster per question than the best specialist, rising to 6.4 times with batching.
citing_sentences: With batching the median rises to 6.4$\times$ (range 0.8–41$\times$), and the specialist is faster on only 3 rows (See Figure 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: EO capability relative to specialist level. For each setting with a specialist reference, EO-Jev’s score as a percentage of the best open EO specialist’s. Settings are grouped into tiers: exceeds specialist level (above 110%), at specialist level (100–110%) and approaching (85–100%). No setting falls below 85%. Bars beyond 165% are clipped. Badges: I = in-domain, O = out-of-domain.
figures.headline: Fifteen settings exceed the best specialist by over 10 percent, and no setting falls below 85 percent of specialist level.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 summarizes where EO-Jev stands relative to the strongest available open EO specialist on each setting.

abstract: Earth observation (EO) workflows require selecting among known outcomes, estimating confidence, and processing large volumes of imagery. Generative vision-language models can address these tasks, but autoregressive decoding is computationally costly and their confidence estimates are unreliable. Decision models offer an alternative, returning probabilities over candidate answers in a single forward pass. However, their accuracy, calibration, and transfer across EO tasks remain insufficiently understood. We investigate these properties through a diagnostic study of d3-flash (8.4B parameters) across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks. We find that compositional reasoning transfers well and calibration improves over its Qwen3.5-9B backbone on 24 settings, while counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain challenging. To address these limitations, we adapt d3-flash through low-rank fine-tuning on public EO training splits, producing EO-Jev. EO-Jev improves significantly over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28. It also achieves an average gain of 8.0 points across 12 held-out settings and lower expected calibration error than specialists on 21 of 28 settings. These improvements come at a modest cost of 1.8 points in general decision performance. Our results demonstrate the potential of adapting general decision models into competitive EO generalists while highlighting persistent challenges in quantitative perception, option-order consistency, and calibration under distribution shift.

sections.body: Decision models return a probability over candidate answers in one forward pass instead of generating text. The authors note that no general decision model had been evaluated on remote-sensing data, and the closest prior work trained and evaluated separately on each benchmark. The paper therefore studies d3-flash, an 8.4B-parameter decision model built on Qwen3.5-9B, across 30 settings from 23 public benchmarks. It addresses four questions: which capabilities transfer, how Earth observation supervision changes performance, how calibration and inference cost compare, and which limitations persist.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Decision models return option probabilities in one pass, but their accuracy and calibration on Earth observation are unclear.

sections.body: Each setting is run on identical images, questions and candidate answers for d3-flash, its Qwen3.5-9B backbone and the best open-weight Earth observation specialist per dataset. Settings are labelled in-domain (18) or out-of-domain (12), depending on whether EO-Jev trained on images from the same dataset. Accuracy is the main metric, with exact-set match for multi-select items, strict CircularEval for LHRS-Bench and correct abstention for VHM deceptive questions. Calibration is measured by expected calibration error with 15 equal-width bins. Differences between EO-Jev and d3-flash use a paired 95% bootstrap over images.
sections.heading: Evaluation Setup
sections.headline: The evaluation compares d3-flash, its backbone and specialists on identical questions across 30 settings from public benchmarks.

sections.body: On LHRS-Bench under strict CircularEval, d3-flash scores 77.5 against 60.0 for the best specialist, and on CHOICE it scores 83.5 against 76.9. It trails specialists on scene and visual question answering benchmarks, reaching 78.1 on AID against 98.5 for RSThinker. Counting, change, damage and absent-object tasks are weak: xBD damage accuracy is 41.1 against a chance level of 25.0, and correct abstention on VHM deceptive questions is 30.4%. Compared with its backbone, d3-flash has lower expected calibration error in 24 of 30 settings, though its accuracy gains are generally modest.
sections.heading: How Far Does a General Decision Model Reach on EO?
sections.headline: A general decision model transfers well on multiple-choice reasoning but trails on counting, change, damage and absent objects.

sections.body: Low-rank adaptation on public Earth observation training splits improves all 18 in-domain settings, by 23.8 points on average (median 24.6). Of the 12 out-of-domain settings, 8 improve significantly, by 8.0 points on average. Correct abstention on VHM deceptive questions rises from 30.4 to 74.0 even though no VHM data was used. EO-Jev matches or exceeds the best specialist on 20 of 28 settings. CHOICE (-1.5) and LHRS-Bench strict (-5.2) decrease significantly. The general Decision Index falls from 93.7 to 91.9, a drop of 1.8 points.
sections.heading: What Does EO Supervision Add?
sections.headline: EO adaptation lifts in-domain and held-out settings, matching or exceeding specialists on 20 of 28 settings at a 1.8 point general cost.

sections.body: EO-Jev has significantly lower expected calibration error than d3-flash on 17 of 30 settings, higher on 5, and no significant change on 8. Against the best specialist, its calibration error is lower on 21 of 28 settings. Specialist probabilities are poorly calibrated on counting and multi-select tasks, with RSThinker at 0.712 on NWPU VHR-10. Where EO-Jev is significantly less calibrated than d3-flash, its mean confidence exceeds its accuracy. With one question per call, EO-Jev is a median 3.2 times faster than the best specialist, and 6.4 times faster with batching.
sections.heading: Can the Model’s Confidence Be Trusted, and at What Cost?
sections.headline: EO-Jev's calibration error is lower than specialists' on 21 of 28 settings, and its single pass is faster.

sections.body: Counting on out-of-domain NWPU VHR-10 reaches 72.0, trailing RSThinker by 7.8 points, and reaches 47.7 on in-domain DOTA-v2, with absolute accuracy still low. Adaptation slightly erodes option-order consistency, with LHRS-Bench strict accuracy down 5.2 points. UrBench does not change significantly, moving from 60.3 to 61.5, because the training data has no cross-view supervision. EO-Jev becomes overconfident on SIRI-WHU, GEOBench-VLM, fMoW-WILDS continent and VHM honest questions, mostly out of domain. The authors propose option-permutation augmentation as a remedy and leave temperature scaling for future work.
sections.heading: What Remains Hard?
sections.headline: Counting on unseen imagery, option-order consistency, cross-view geometry and overconfidence under shift remain unresolved.

sections.body: Fifteen settings exceed specialist level by more than 10%, mostly in disaster assessment, change and temporal reasoning, geo-localization and fine-grained recognition. Five are at specialist level and eight are approaching it. No setting shows a substantial gap. The authors propose a division of labor: a calibrated decision model handles most questions in one forward pass, with thresholded deferral of uncertain cases. Specialists remain useful for counting on unfamiliar imagery and where generated explanations matter more than calibrated confidence.
sections.heading: Where Does a Decision Model Stand on EO?
sections.headline: A calibrated decision model can serve as the default EO interface, with uncertain answers deferred to specialists.

sections.body: The appendix lists benchmarks by capability group and the specialist reference for each setting in Table 2. It describes output processing: specialists are scored either by option probabilities read from a prefilled answer or by greedy generation mapped to an option. EO-Jev training examples come only from public training splits, with all evaluation images removed, including AID images outside the evaluation list, EuroSAT and BigEarthNet v2 training splits, and xBD train and tier3 splits. Timing runs on one exclusive node with 4×A100-80GB GPUs in BF16, using a seeded sample of 160 questions per row.
sections.heading: Additional Evaluation Details
sections.headline: Appendix lists benchmarks, specialist references, output processing, EO-Jev training sources and the timing protocol.

sections.body: The diagnostic study finds that d3-flash transfers well to several compositional reasoning tasks and generally improves calibration over its backbone, but remains limited on counting, change quantification, damage grading and absent objects. EO-Jev improves significantly on 26 settings and matches or exceeds the specialist reference on 20 of 28, with an average gain of 8.0 percentage points on 12 held-out settings. Costs include a 1.8 point drop in general decision performance, lower accuracy on two reasoning benchmarks and higher calibration error on some settings. The authors name quantitative and geometric perception and option-order consistency as priorities.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Adapting d3-flash yields EO-Jev, which improves 26 settings at a 1.8 point cost in general decision performance.
